01

Cloud gaming is rented. I wanted to own mine.

Cloud gaming is usually expensive, closed, or both. I wanted the opposite: my PC, my saves, my network, reachable from anywhere.

Streaming itself is the solved part. Sunshine handles it well. The hard part is everything around it: starting and stopping sessions cleanly, keeping saves safe from one session to the next, knowing when the host is unhealthy, and fixing it when I am not there.

  • Session management
  • Save synchronisation
  • Host monitoring
  • Recovery when things fail
02

Four layers, one host.

Dashboard.
One React app. After login it shows the full admin dashboard or a scoped user dashboard limited to that account's own sessions, analytics, history and logs.
Backend.
FastAPI. Every route except login and first-run bootstrap needs a valid JWT, and roles are enforced per route.
Host agent.
The Python layer that touches the machine: runs sessions, injects and backs up saves, monitors, validates and performs recovery actions.
Storage.
History, users and recovery events live in SQLite. Host config, the game library and the active-session crash snapshot stay as JSON on purpose, so the host can still recover when the database is the thing that broke.

Single host today. A multi-host design exists as a document, not as code.

03

What went wrong, and what I learned.

These are the problems that taught me the most. Each one links to the full write-up.

Tailscale is not a service you restart

Problem
Tailscale looked healthy to Windows while the connection was dead. My first watchdog just restarted the service and often fixed nothing.
What I found
After about a week of testing: Tailscale is two parts, the service and the IPN backend process, and a healthy connection needs both. Different failure states needed different fixes.
What I did
Rebuilt the watchdog as detect, diagnose, classify, then act: run tailscale up when stopped, start the Tailscale process when unavailable, start tailscale-ipn.exe when there is no state. Login failures are deliberately left alone.
Why
A fix that is right for one failure state is wrong for another. Recovery has to start from diagnosis.
Full write-up →

Live save sync that quietly never ran

Problem
After I made save-file matching configurable per game, live sync stopped. No errors, just silence. The final cleanup still captured saves correctly.
What I found
Hashing, capture and verification all worked, so my first suspect was wrong. The real cause was an incomplete migration: live sync belonged to the old command-line session runner and never made it into the new FastAPI execution path.
What I did
Moved the live-sync lifecycle into the service path that actually runs sessions.
Why
When a bug survives your first three theories, check the architecture, not the algorithm.
Full write-up →

Stale dashboard, correct backend

Problem
Session analytics, host metrics and recovery events sometimes showed old data.
What I found
I suspected WebSockets and React state. Calling the API directly returned correct data every time. The browser was caching the high-frequency monitoring endpoints.
What I did
Disabled caching on both sides: response headers from the backend and no-cache requests from the frontend.
Why
Measure at the boundary first. Testing the API alone cut the search space in half.
Full write-up →

Authenticating a caller that is not a user

Problem
Once everything required a login, four endpoints still had to be callable by two non-user callers: Sunshine's stream hook script and a thread that tails Sunshine's log.
What I found
The hook runs as a separate OS process, so there is no Python call stack to check. The only enforcement point left is the request itself.
What I did
A single-purpose shared secret, generated with secrets.token_urlsafe(32), sent as X-Internal-Event-Token, checked with hmac.compare_digest, attached to exactly four routes, and never accepted anywhere else.
Why
Leaving those routes open would let any logged-in user spoof stream state. A narrow credential keeps the blast radius small.
Full write-up →

Backups that multiplied, sessions that outlived a crash

Problem
Early on, every sync could create another save backup, and a backend crash could leave sessions stuck in a half-finished state.
What I found
Both came from not being able to tell meaningful change from noise, and from state that lived only in memory.
What I did
Hash-based change detection so identical saves are not backed up again, and startup recovery that restores consistency from a small JSON snapshot after a crash.
Why
Reliability work is mostly deciding what must survive a failure, and writing that down before it fails.
Full write-up →

05

What v0.1 actually does.

  • Sessions

    Lifecycle management, timers, event logging, analytics, cleanup workflows

  • Saves

    Injection, backup, restore, archives, live sync, hash-based change detection

  • Monitoring

    CPU, RAM and disk, host readiness validation

  • Recovery

    Sunshine watchdog, Tailscale recovery, recovery statistics and events, stale-session recovery on startup

  • Access

    JWT login with first-run admin bootstrap, admin and user roles on every route, user management, password change

08

Honest status.

Done

v0.1 host foundation, then Phase 23 session persistence and reconnection, Phase 24 authentication and roles, Phase 25 the move from JSON files to SQLite.

Next

Phase 26 a dedicated user app, 27 embedded Tailscale, 28 Moonlight automation, 29 production player experience, 30 production host dashboard, 31 security and audit logging, 32 deployment and packaging.

Not done yet

  • No refresh tokens: sessions expire and need a new login.
  • No login rate limiting or account lockout.
  • No audit log of logins or admin actions (planned, Phase 31).
  • The API only allows localhost origins until it is deployed somewhere else.
  • No automated backend tests yet.
